A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same vulnerability-game study despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, allowing additions, removals, and relocated material to be matched reliably.

before.justification: V1 reports original RL experiments, cross-task transfer, SFT distillation, corrective training, and appendix controls using Qwen and Llama models.

after.justification: V2 retains these original experiments and adds a source-task exposure control, corrective-training trajectories, and HarmBench/TruthfulQA evaluations.

M1.justification: The four games, GRPO training, sequential RL, SFT distillation, and Safety GRPO remain unchanged. Protected score-field overwriting through insecure parsing was already described in v1 Section 3.4 and Appendix C.4; v2's revised summaries do not establish a new mechanism.

E1.justification: Appendix A.7 adds HarmBench and TruthfulQA checks of original and exploit-trained checkpoints, extending evaluation to broader alignment outcomes. The four vulnerability games and their existing BBEH, CNN/DailyMail, and LiveCodeBench coverage remain.

E2.justification: Appendix A.5/Table 12 adds initialization through SFT on correct, non-exploitative Reward Tampering solutions to the Qwen3-4B-Base sequential-training comparison. From-scratch and exploit-RL initializations were already evaluated; the existing main comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: Table 2 and Appendix D replace the refusal-rate-difference definition with the fraction of paired refuse-audit/answer-user outcomes, resolving inconsistency with v1 Section 3.1. Appendix A.5 also introduces the non-exploit SFT initialization protocol. These reported changes do not establish that existing evaluations were rerun.

E4.justification: V2 adds a source-exposure control, trajectories for the existing correction experiment, and broad-alignment diagnostics in Appendices A.5–A.7. These extend the transfer and persistence analyses without replacing them. V1's detailed E.4 Reward Tampering transcript is removed, while the separate illustrated tampering case remains.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Appendix A.1 retains 16 rollouts per prompt. The new correction curves show trajectories without introducing uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Matched numerical entries in v1 Tables 3–10 and v2 Tables 4–11 are unchanged. New Table 12 reports 80.7% exploitation for the non-exploit SFT control alongside the existing 81.6% from-scratch and 89.8% exploit-RL results. Table 13 adds broad-alignment scores, and Figure 3 adds correction trajectories.

T1.justification: Appendix C.2 corrects the self-grading argument: v1 checks whether overclaiming has nonnegative return, whereas v2 explicitly derives E_overclaim − E_honest = (1−q)(1−7p). This establishes the advantage over honest reporting for p < 1/7 and q < 1. The experimental audit probability remains 0.1.

C1.justification: V1 claims to introduce a distinct alignment-risk category and broadly transferable exploit skills. V2 recasts the contribution as a controlled framework for vulnerable RL pipelines, explicitly limits transfer, and elevates task-dependent resistance to correction into the abstract and main contributions. This substantively narrows and redefines the claimed contribution.

C2.justification: V2 substantially qualifies explanations involving internalization, situational awareness, and capability-driven generalization. Sections 5.5–6 and Appendix A acknowledge reversed RL-versus-SFT comparisons, persistent tampering under both origins, nonmonotonic scaling, and limitations of loophole removal. New broad-alignment checks support a mostly task-bounded interpretation.

D1.justification: The code-access link changes from Capability_Oriented_Alignment_Risk to Capability-seeking-RL-risk. Removing v1 Appendix E.4 also removes a worked prompt/output example, although Appendix F retains the tampering templates. Existing audit settings, rewriting model pool, and processing details are largely preserved.

R1.justification: Section 2 now positions the study as complementary to prior reward-hacking and scheming research instead of encompassing those behaviors within a broader category. Section 6 adds connections to EVOL-RL and TTRL. References also add safety-related work and remove the earlier jailbreak-defense and semantically-aware-reward citations.

P1.justification: The title and terminology change throughout, with extensive rewriting of the abstract, introduction, result explanations, discussion, conclusion, impact statement, and analytical appendices. Research questions and headings emphasize discovery, bounded transfer, and persistence. This exceeds localized editing despite retaining the overall section hierarchy.

P2.justification: V2 extensively reformats the main text into two columns and changes table and figure sizing and placement. It adds conceptual Figure 1, correction Figure 3, and Tables 12–13; Table 3 redisplays existing results. V1 Figure 1 is retained as appendix Figure 4.

improvement.justification: V2 makes the conclusions more defensible by acknowledging counterexamples in retained results and correcting Appendix C.2's reward comparison. New controls and broader alignment checks provide useful supporting evidence. The gains remain limited: the source-exposure control compares SFT with RL, so it does not fully isolate exploit experience, and the new evaluations lack detailed protocol and uncertainty reporting.
